analysis.one_liner: Shields manufacturers from most lawsuits when another person's crime or a lawful sale caused the harm.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a vote: it was referred to two House committees and a subcommittee in 2001 and died there when Congress ended in January 2003.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would rewrite product liability rules nationwide for anything made or sold across state lines. If someone else's crime or intentional wrongdoing partly caused an injury, the manufacturer could not be sued for it, even in state court. Manufacturers also could not be sued over how they sold or marketed a product unless they broke a specific statute, and the bill would override any state law that gives manufacturers less protection. It applied to every case filed after it became law.
analysis.who_benefits: Manufacturers of virtually any product that moves in interstate commerce. They would gain a shield against lawsuits where a third party's criminal act contributed to the harm, and against suits over sales or marketing practices that complied with existing statutes. The shield would apply even in state courts, overriding state laws that currently allow such suits.

how_it_helps.text: Manufacturers would not be liable for harm if a proximate cause was a criminal or intentionally tortious act by someone other than the manufacturer, in either state or federal court.

Manufacturers would not be liable for harm from the sale or marketing of a product unless they failed to substantially comply with a state or federal statute governing that sale or marketing, and that failure proximately caused the harm.
The bill preempts inconsistent state law but preserves any state law that gives manufacturers greater protection, so the legal floor nationwide would shift toward manufacturers.

analysis.who_pays: People injured by products. If a criminal or intentional act by anyone else contributed to the injury, they could not recover from the manufacturer even if the product itself was defective. Suits over how a product was sold or marketed would survive only if the manufacturer broke a specific statute. State courts would lose the power to apply their own liability rules.

drawbacks.text: An injured person could be barred from recovering from a manufacturer whenever a third party's crime or intentional act was a proximate cause of the harm, even if the product was defective or the manufacturer's conduct contributed.
Suit over a product's sale or marketing would survive only if the manufacturer violated a specific statute, so common-law claims about deceptive or unsafe marketing would be cut off.
The bill preempts state tort law nationwide, removing states' traditional authority to set the rules for injury cases within their borders.

A good-faith objection supporters would raise: liability rules vary across states and manufacturers can face suits even when a third party's criminal misuse caused the harm, which they argued burdens interstate commerce.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill's benefits would flow almost entirely to manufacturers in the form of a broad shield from product liability suits, including suits in state courts. The costs would fall on people injured by defective products, who would lose compensation whenever a third party's criminal or intentional act was a proximate cause of their harm, and on states, which would lose control over their own tort rules. The strongest argument for it — uniform rules for national commerce — is real, but the remedy here was one-sided: it barred suits without adding any substitute protection for injured consumers.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in May 2001, sent to the Judiciary and Energy and Commerce committees, referred to a subcommittee a few weeks later, and never received a hearing, markup, or floor vote before Congress ended in January 2003.

narrative.text: Rep. John Hostettler introduced the bill on May 23, 2001, with six original cosponsors.
The House referred it to the Judiciary Committee and to the Energy and Commerce Committee the same day.
On June 8, 2001, it was referred to the Commerce, Trade and Consumer Protection subcommittee, and the record shows no further action.
The 107th Congress ended January 3, 2003, with the bill still in committee and no vote ever taken in either chamber.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Injured consumers kept their existing right to sue manufacturers under state tort law, and no manufacturer liability shield took effect. The bill's backers did not get the nationwide preemption they sought.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Injured consumers kept their right to sue

sides.party_line_note: Support was overwhelmingly Republican: 12 of 223 House Republicans cosponsored, versus 1 of 208 House Democrats and the chamber's single Independent.

industries.industry: Product manufacturers (consumer goods, appliances, equipment, and other manufactured products sold across state lines)
industries.note: Had it passed, the bill would have given manufacturers a nationwide shield from suits over defective products whenever a third party's crime contributed to the harm, and from suits over lawful sales and marketing. It never passed, so manufacturers remain subject to state product liability law.

industries.industry: Trial lawyers and consumer plaintiffs' bar
industries.note: The bill would have narrowed the pool of viable injury suits, which would have cost plaintiff lawyers work and injured clients compensation. Because it died, existing state tort remedies remain intact.
A manufacturer liability shield would have reduced manufacturers' exposure and insurers' payouts on product claims. The bill's failure leaves the existing insurance market unchanged.
